title: Climate Models Accurately Predict Ocean‐Going Meltwater Runoff From the Northwest Greenland Ice Sheet
content:
Abstract

Climatic surface mass balance (SMB) meltwater runoff models are used to estimate current and future Greenland Ice Sheet sea level contributions. However, comparisons between SMB model runoff and in situ proglacial river discharge observations show large discrepancies. Most studies are from Southwest Greenland, where active subglacial systems and proglacial lakes complicate direct comparisons between SMB runoff and proglacial discharge observations. We present and compare four years (2019–2022) of new in situ proglacial discharge observations from two watersheds in Northwest Greenland having no subglacial interference and no proglacial lakes, and three years of new data (2019–2021) from three watersheds in Southwest Greenland with active subglacial systems and proglacial lakes. For the three largest watersheds, we compare observed proglacial discharge with daily RACMO2.3p2, MARv3.14, and MERRA-2 SMB estimates. Examination of all five records finds fast meltwater evacuation in the Northwest watersheds and regional systems of runoff behavior. In the Northwest, we find broad agreement between modeled and observed daily runoff (−21%, 6%, and −6% error for RACMO2.3p2, MARv3.14, and MERRA-2, respectively). In the Southwest, we find higher uncertainty due to high potentiometric watershed uncertainty (−14%–90%, −6%–120%, and −37%–62% error, respectively, for SW 474) and runoff overestimation (13%–31%, 97%–137%, and 68%–103%, respectively, for SW 474). Alignment of SMB and in situ hydrographs from the Northwest Greenland Ice Sheet, ideal for model validation, suggests that climate models correctly estimate Greenland Ice Sheet runoff contributions to the global ocean where subglacial activity and subglacial lakes are absent.
